claims.claim: The main narrative of The Origins of Totalitarianism is a getting free of processes which demolish the artificial public realm of European nation-states.
claims.supporting_excerpt: it is enough, for the aim of this paper, to remind that the main narrative of The Origins of Totalitarianism is a getting free of processes which demolish the building of European nation-states erected in the former centuries. In the nation states, in the terms of the Arendtian political philosophy, an artifice of public realm as a stage for action had been created and maintained. But the aggressive unleashed processes of the 20th century destroyed this artificial public realm.

claims.claim: In The Human Condition, Arendt's implicit presupposition is that despite the defeat of Nazi totalitarianism, the processes of re-naturalization continue to endanger the shrinking artificial man-made world.
claims.supporting_excerpt: In The Human Condition Arendt is conspicuously silent about totalitarianism; the term itself appears only once during the argumentation (Arendt 1958: 216). But the implicit presupposition of the book is Arendt’s deep conviction that, in spite of the defeat of Nazi totalitarianism, the threat is not over; the processes of re-naturalization are endangering the shrinking terrain of artificial, man-made world.

must_not_be_lost: The connection drawn between totalitarianism as a process of re-naturalization and the ongoing threats to the man-made world in The Human Condition.
output.segment_function: The block analyzes the transition from cultural criticism to political philosophy in Arendt's work, linking the concept of process and re-naturalization in The Origins of Totalitarianism to the implicit threats facing the artificial human world in The Human Condition.
